lesson.title: The Reverse Journey: Cooling Curves and Supercooling
lesson.summary: A cooling curve is the mirror image of a heating curve, tracking heat released as a substance cools and changes phase, with a notable exception when supercooling delays freezing.
lesson.body:
A cooling curve tracks the same variables as a heating curve, temperature against heat removed, but runs in the opposite direction: starting from a gas or hot liquid and ending at a cold solid. Structurally, it has the same shape as a heating curve turned around: sloped segments where temperature drops as heat leaves the sample within a single phase, and flat plateaus where temperature holds steady while heat leaves during a phase change, condensation and freezing, releasing the latent heat that was absorbed during the corresponding heating process.

Every value on a cooling curve is, in principle, identical in magnitude to the matching value on the heating curve for the same substance and mass, just with the sign flipped: heat is leaving the system, exothermic, rather than entering it, endothermic. The specific heat capacities and latent heats of fusion and vaporization are properties of the substance itself, not of which direction the temperature is moving, so a plateau during freezing releases exactly as much energy per gram as the corresponding plateau during melting absorbed.

There is one asymmetry worth knowing about: supercooling. On an idealized cooling curve, temperature should hold perfectly flat at the freezing point during the entire freezing plateau. In real experiments, especially with pure, undisturbed liquids, temperature can actually dip a little below the true freezing point before crystals begin to form, because nucleation, the formation of the first stable crystal, requires molecules to randomly arrange themselves into the right structure, which does not always happen instantly right at the freezing point. Once nucleation finally occurs, crystallization proceeds rapidly and releases latent heat fast enough that the temperature jumps back up to the true freezing point and then holds there for the remainder of the freezing plateau, a small but real dip then recovery visible as a brief notch near the start of the plateau on an actual recorded cooling curve. This is the same supercooling phenomenon introduced in the melting and freezing chapter, now visible as a specific, recognizable feature on a graph.

How much heat is released as 40.0 g of liquid water, freshly condensed from steam, cools from 100.0 C down to 60.0 C, remaining liquid the entire time? Using q = mcDeltaT with c = 4.184 J/(g C) and a temperature decrease of 40.0 C: q = (40.0 g)(4.184 J/g C)(40.0 C) = 6,694.4 J, about 6.69 kJ released to the surroundings. Notice this is the same style of calculation as the heating curve example in the previous chapter, just describing heat flowing out of the sample and into its surroundings rather than in.
